title: China’s Quiet Bet on Methanol Is Paying Off
gist: A short excerpt of a Foreign Policy op-ed arguing that Geely now runs one of the world's largest methanol-powered commercial vehicle fleets — the payoff of a technology pathway Ford started with China in 1995 and then abandoned — and that tech leadership depends on whether governments, firms and institutions keep multiple pathways alive long enough for one to mature.

themes.theme: Methanol as China's overlooked clean-transport lane

insights.claim: Geely operates one of the world's largest fleets of methanol-powered commercial vehicles, making methanol flex-fuel a live but under-covered part of China's clean transport story alongside battery EVs.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Watch methanol fuel infrastructure and heavy-duty flex-fuel commercial vehicle demand in China as a second, non-battery decarbonization channel that most EV-focused models ignore.
insights.quote: Geely now operates one of the world’s largest fleets of methanol-powered commercial vehicles
insights.locator: China is an electric vehicle giant

insights.claim: BYD and Geely are described as dominating global electric vehicle markets, making China the reference point for clean transport scale.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Baseline for any China auto-export thesis: the same firms leading batteries are also the ones carrying the alternative-fuel option.
insights.locator: China is an electric vehicle giant

insights.claim: Methanol vehicles in China trace back to a 1995 collaboration with Ford that produced no commercial breakthrough and was abandoned by Ford, yet the technology resurfaced in China nearly three decades later.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete case that abandoned R&D pathways can be revived by a partner with longer patience — relevant when judging which shelved Western technologies could reappear as Chinese export categories.
insights.quote: Ford eventually abandoned methanol, while China moved on to other technologies.
insights.locator: That story begins with an almost forgotten collaboration

themes.theme: Optionality as the real driver of tech leadership

insights.claim: Technology leadership depends less on the technology itself than on whether governments, firms and local institutions will sustain multiple technological pathways long enough for one of them to mature.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Use pathway persistence — not current unit economics — as the screen for which national innovation systems will own the next transport or energy standard.
insights.quote: a critical element is whether governments, firms, and local institutions are willing to sustain multiple technological pathways long enough for one of them to mature
insights.locator: Tech leadership, especially in Big Tech forms

insights.claim: The implied verdict on the U.S. side is that Ford's exit from methanol was a strategic option abandoned rather than a technology that failed, since the same pathway later matured in Chinese hands.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Argues for valuing long-duration industrial policy and R&D option value when comparing U.S. and Chinese clean-transport positioning.
insights.locator: The partnership never produced a commercial breakthrough
